\section{Three Scenarios for the Lending Environment}
\label{sec:scenarios}
\label{sec:levers}

This section answers RQ3: how bureau visibility and mandatory affordability screening change simulated borrowing and distress, with and without peer influence on adoption.
The benchmark scenario is the pre-2026 position, in which \ac{BNPL} obligations are invisible to the bureau and originations pass only a light screen.
Each of two regulatory switches defines a further scenario, and one behavioural setting is varied across all three:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Bureau visibility} ($\mathbb{1}^{\text{bur}}$): \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the traditional lender's Regulation 23A test. This is the affordability channel of the 2026 reporting requirement \cite{businessday_bnpl_2026}; the scoring channel is outside the model (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}).
\item \textbf{Mandatory affordability screening} ($\mathbb{1}^{\text{aff}}$): the Regulation 23A test is applied to \ac{BNPL} originations, the South African analogue of the \ac{FCA}'s proportionate affordability check \cite{fca_ps26_1, woolard2021}.
\item \textbf{Peer influence} ($\beta$): every arm is run at $\beta = 0$ and at $\beta = 1$ (Equation~\ref{eq:peer}). Peer influence is a behavioural setting, not a regulatory switch. It is varied to test whether the regulatory results depend on how adoption spreads.
\end{enumerate}
The light screen in the benchmark is a modelling assumption.
Whether an agreement that levies late fees is incidental credit, and which provisions would then apply, is a legal question that the scenarios do not settle (Section~\ref{sec:background}).

Table~\ref{tab:scenarios} reports the outcomes and Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios} plots default and cumulative volume.
Differences are scenario less benchmark at the same $\beta$ and carry one unpaired standard error.
As in Section~\ref{sec:results}, a difference is described as detectable only when it exceeds two standard errors, and $\beta = 0$ is the better guide to magnitudes (Section~\ref{sec:results-injection}).
Cumulative volume is reported beside default because a rule that only delays borrowing within the horizon leaves it unchanged, whereas a rule that prevents borrowing lowers it.
The table notes call this the defer-versus-desist criterion.

Bureau visibility does not lower default in the affordability channel.
At $\beta = 0$ it raises default by $0.26 \pm 0.11$ percentage points, which is detectable.
At $\beta = 1$ the change is $0.04 \pm 0.12$ points, which is not detectable.
Once \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the Regulation 23A test, the traditional lender refuses more applications: 1{,}160 against 1{,}033 at $\beta = 0$.
A household refused credit that it sought for a shortfall is left with the shortfall, which is one route to higher default.
The refusal count does not by itself explain the increase.
The traditional lender's refusals rise by as much at $\beta = 1$, from 1{,}039 to 1{,}162, and by more under screening, and default does not change detectably in either case.
The outcomes are population aggregates, so they do not show which refused households later default.
The 90+ day arrears share among credit-active households does not change detectably ($-0.06 \pm 0.13$ points at $\beta = 0$).
Cumulative \ac{BNPL} volume moves by less than 1\% at either value of $\beta$, as expected of a switch that acts on the traditional lender's decision and leaves \ac{BNPL} origination as it was.

Mandatory screening refuses \ac{BNPL} requests that the light screen would grant.
Adoption at the final tick falls from 16.71\% to 15.10\% at $\beta = 0$ and from 65.56\% to 62.97\% at $\beta = 1$.
Cumulative volume is 1.8\% and 1.6\% lower, and only the second difference exceeds two standard errors.
Default does not change detectably: the differences are $+0.02 \pm 0.10$ and $-0.05 \pm 0.10$ points.
One explanation, offered after the fact, is that purchases are sized to each household's discretionary budget, so the requests that fail the test are small.
Another is that the test assesses affordability at origination, whereas sustained distress in the model follows income shocks that outlast the household's buffer (Section~\ref{sec:results-robustness}).
Neither is tested directly, because the outcomes do not follow the screened households.

Both switches leave cumulative volume within 2\% of the benchmark.
The 1.6\% to 1.8\% that screening removes is borrowing not undertaken within the horizon.
The measure cannot show whether those purchases were abandoned or postponed beyond it.

Peer influence raises adoption, volume and default in every scenario.
In the benchmark, adoption at the final tick is 65.56\% at $\beta = 1$ against 16.71\% at $\beta = 0$, and cumulative volume is R64.01 million against R5.44 million.
Default is 0.6 to 0.8 points higher at $\beta = 1$ in every scenario.
Neither switch changes default detectably at $\beta = 1$.
The bureau estimate falls by $0.22 \pm 0.16$ points between $\beta = 0$ and $\beta = 1$, treating the four arms as independent, and the two screening estimates differ by less than 0.1 points.
The comparisons therefore give no evidence that peer influence alters the effect of either switch.
An interaction smaller than two standard errors, 0.32 points for the bureau contrast, would not be detected.

Appendix~\ref{app:levers} reports two further levers, each at both values of $\beta$.
The first is a cap on concurrent agreements, which is hypothetical, since no jurisdiction imposes one.
It refuses any new draw while the household holds balances on the stated number of platforms, so a cap of one allows one agreement at a time and is stricter than a single-platform market.
A cap of two lowers default by $1.01 \pm 0.11$ points at $\beta = 0$ with cumulative volume within 0.4\% of the benchmark, and by $1.47 \pm 0.11$ points at $\beta = 1$ with volume 29.5\% lower (Table~\ref{tab:cap}).
A cap of one lowers default by $1.21 \pm 0.10$ and $1.83 \pm 0.13$ points, with volume 23.7\% and 64.1\% lower.
A cap of three does not change default detectably.
The second lever is a cooling-off window that blocks want-driven purchases for one to four ticks after an order (Table~\ref{tab:cooloff}).
At $\beta = 0$ it does not change default detectably at any length.
At $\beta = 1$ it lowers default by between $0.31 \pm 0.12$ and $0.55 \pm 0.12$ points, while cumulative volume falls by between 43.5\% and 77.6\%.

These results agree with Section~\ref{sec:results-stacking}, in which default responds to the number of obligations a household services at once and not to the number of providers.
Bureau visibility and screening each act on the decision to grant one agreement, and neither detectably lowers default.
The cap limits concurrent borrowing directly, and a cap of two at $\beta = 0$ lowers default with volume within 0.4\% of the benchmark.
No cap arm was run under the alternative borrowing rules of Table~\ref{tab:effect}, so the dependence of this reduction on those rules is untested (Section~\ref{sec:amount}).
The model also has no measure of what a household loses when a purchase or a shortfall loan is refused.

In answer to RQ3, neither switch lowers default in the affordability channel.
Bureau visibility raises default by $0.26 \pm 0.11$ points at $\beta = 0$ and has no detectable effect at $\beta = 1$.
Mandatory screening lowers adoption by 1.6 to 2.6 points and leaves cumulative volume within 2\% of the benchmark, with no detectable effect on default.
These results bound only the channel modelled (Section~\ref{sec:lim-reading}): the reporting requirement may also act through credit scores, pricing and lenders' responses, which the model does not represent.
Of the switches and levers tested, only a cap of one or two lowers default at both values of $\beta$.
The cap is hypothetical, and the result does not establish a regulatory threshold.
